title: The passive
why: The fourth B1 lesson: you learn to recognize the passive, which is everywhere in newspaper headlines, signs and menus. Each active binyan you've seen (pa'al, pi'el, hif'il) has a passive twin: nif'al, pu'al and huf'al.

{"lessons": ["

A passive in a single word

In English, the passive needs extra words: \"was written,\" \"was canceled.\" In Hebrew, one word is enough: you simply switch binyan (the verb pattern you saw in unit 9). The active binyanim pa'al, pi'el and hif'il each have a passive twin (the hitpa'el doesn't):

ActivePassivePronunciationPassive meaning
כָּתַב (pa'al)נִכְתַּב (nif'al)nikhtavwas written
סִפֵּר (pi'el)סֻפַּר (pu'al)suparwas told
הִזְמִין (hif'il)הֻזְמַן (huf'al)huzmanwas invited, was ordered
הַסִּפּוּר הַזֶּה סֻפַּר לִי עַל יְדֵי סַבְתָּא.This story was told to me by my grandmother. [ha-sipur ha-ze supar li al yedei savta]

\"By\" is עַל יְדֵי (al yedei). But in speech, Israelis often prefer the active with a \"they\" that has no subject, just like English \"they\" in \"they opened a new restaurant\": פָּתְחוּ מִסְעָדָה חֲדָשָׁה. You'll come across the passive mostly in writing: newspapers, signs, menus.

In this lesson, the goal is to recognize these forms when you read them, not to produce all of them.

", "

The nif'al: נִ at the start

In the past, you can recognize the nif'al by the נִ at the beginning. It takes the same endings as the past tense you know:

MasculineFemininePlural
נִפְתַּח niftakhנִפְתְּחָה niftekhaנִפְתְּחוּ niftekhu
נִסְגַּר nisgarנִסְגְּרָה nisgeraנִסְגְּרוּ nisgeru
נִכְתַּב nikhtavנִכְתְּבָה nikhtevaנִכְתְּבוּ nikhtevu
סִפְרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה נִפְתְּחָה בְּחֵיפָה.A new library opened in Haifa. [sifriya khadasha niftekha be-Kheyfa]

The nif'al often matches an English verb used without an object: \"the door opens,\" \"the store closes,\" or \"is found / is located\" (נִמְצָא, was found or is located). In the present, you'll read it on store doors:

הַחֲנוּת נִפְתַּחַת בְּתֵשַׁע וְנִסְגֶּרֶת בְּשֶׁבַע.The store opens at nine and closes at seven. [ha-khanut niftakhat be-tesha ve-nisgeret be-sheva]

The trap: a נִ at the beginning can also be the \"we\" of the future. נִכְתֹּב (we will write) and נִכְתַּב (was written) differ by just one vowel, o or a. In a newspaper without vowels, the meaning of the sentence decides.

", "

Pu'al and huf'al: the \"u\" sound

The pu'al (passive of the pi'el) and the huf'al (passive of the hif'il) have something in common that's easy to spot: the u sound (as in \"rule\") under the first letter (the kubutz, three diagonal dots).

ActivePassivePronunciationMeaning
בִּטֵּלבֻּטַּלbutalwas canceled
שִׁפֵּץשֻׁפַּץshupatswas renovated
הִזְמִיןהֻזְמַןhuzmanwas invited, ordered
הִגִּישׁהֻגַּשׁhugashwas served
הַקּוֹנְצֶרְט בַּפַּארְק בֻּטַּל בִּגְלַל הַגֶּשֶׁם.The concert in the park was canceled because of the rain. [ha-kontsert ba-park butal biglal ha-geshem]
כָּל הַתּוֹשָׁבִים הֻזְמְנוּ לַחֲגִיגָה בַּכִּכָּר.All the residents were invited to the celebration in the square. [kol ha-toshavim huzmenu la-khagiga ba-kikar]

In the present, these passives start with מְ or מֻ and are often used as adjectives: מְשֻׁפָּץ (renovated), מֻזְמָן (invited). At a hotel, you'll read:

אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר מֻגֶּשֶׁת עַד הַשָּׁעָה עֶשֶׂר.Breakfast is served until ten. [arukhat ha-boker mugeshet ad ha-sha'a eser]

In newspapers, without niqqud, this \"u\" sound is written with a ו (full spelling). So a ו right after the first letter of a verb is a good clue that it's a pu'al or a huf'al.
